mainEntity.name: Our therapists wipe the tables and mats between patients. Is that enough?

acceptedAnswer.text: Wiping is cleaning, and cleaning is not disinfection. They are two steps. Treatment tables, mats, weights, and bands that contact intact skin are non-critical items that need to be cleaned and then disinfected between patients at the level the degree of soiling requires, per the CDC Infection Prevention Checklist non-critical item definition and CDC Core Practices 5f. Between-patient turnover stays with your clinicians, because they are the ones in the room. What we own is the end-of-day terminal pass across every table, mat, and plinth, plus floors, restrooms, and shared areas.

mainEntity.name: Nobody here checks whether cleaning was done properly. Should we be?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, and the absence of checking is itself a finding. Section I item D of the CDC Infection Prevention Checklist expects evidence that the clinic monitors and assesses whether cleaning is consistently and correctly performed. We build that in: dated service logs by zone, a supervisor audit on a defined interval using a written checklist tied to your own protocol, and a corrective-action note whenever something misses. You keep the record. The point is not to grade our crew for you, it is that you can show an assessor a monitoring process that exists on paper.

mainEntity.name: What documentation do I get for a CARF survey or a DPH review?

acceptedAnswer.text: The written cleaning and disinfection policy covering the gym, treatment tables, and shared equipment, with responsibility assigned line by line; the equipment inventory flagging items with no manufacturer reprocessing instructions; the product list with EPA registration numbers and label contact times; SDS sheets; per-person training and competency records; dated service logs; and supervisor audit results. That set answers Section I items A through D of the CDC Infection Prevention Checklist directly. Dory's carries $2 million in general liability and will name your clinic on the certificate.

Rehabilitation Clinic Cleaning for Spencer facilities

In a rehabilitation clinic, most cleaning failures happen at treatment tables, mats, therabands, free weights, exercise balls, parallel bars, treadmills. That is where our Spencer crews start, because the underlying risk is direct skin contact with shared equipment all day, with no barrier — MRSA and fungal transfer.

  • Physical Therapy
  • Occupational Therapy
  • Speech Therapy
  • Sports Medicine

Usually arranged with the clinic director (pt / ot / speech).

Inside a Spencer service visit

Where contamination concentrates

  • Treatment tables and plinths
  • Exercise mats
  • Free weights, dumbbells and kettlebells
  • Resistance bands and handles
  • Treadmill and bike handles and consoles
  • Parallel bars and balance equipment

Our sequence, step by step

  1. Agree which equipment staff wipe between patients and which the cleaning crew handles at end of day.
  2. Launder or replace reusable linens per the clinic's process — we do not take clinic linens off site unless contracted.
  3. Empty trash; sharps are rare but stay with the clinic's hauler if present.
  4. Damp-mop gym floors and vacuum carpeted areas.
  5. Log areas completed and any damaged equipment surfaces we notice.

How often

  • Treatment tables and shared equipment: between patients by staff, full clean daily.
  • Gym floor: daily.
  • Periodic: equipment deep clean and high dusting.

Clinics with early-morning patients may prefer a pre-opening clean.

Documentation you receive

  • Product list with EPA registration numbers and contact times
  • Safety Data Sheets
  • Signed service logs
  • Certificate of insurance

What inspectors cite — and how we prevent it

Real, published regulatory findings — every citation links to its source.

CDC Infection Prevention Checklist for Outpatient Settings, Section I Environmental Cleaning item A

No written policies and procedures for routine cleaning and disinfection of the gym, treatment tables and shared equipment, including who is responsible for what.

CDC Infection Prevention Checklist for Outpatient Settings, Section I item B

Cleaning staff have not received job-specific training and competency validation at hire and whenever procedures or products change.

CDC Infection Prevention Checklist for Outpatient Settings, non-critical item definition; CDC Core Infection Prevention and Control Practices 5f

Treatment tables, mats, weights and bands that contact intact skin are wiped but not cleaned and then disinfected between patients at the level the degree of soiling requires.
